title: Is the competitive power market model broken? | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Energy Gang show notes framing a live policy fight: US electricity prices are rising well above inflation as data centre demand collides with a system designed for a different era, and Exelon's Carim Khouzami argues regulated utilities barred by state rules from owning generation should be allowed to run their own power plants. PJM is the test case — its affordability and reliability strains have drawn attention from state governors, federal regulators and the White House, while Amy Myers Jaffe counters with overbuild risk and whether batteries are getting a fair shot to compete.

themes.theme: Price inflation and the political trigger

insights.claim: US electricity prices are rising at well above the general rate of inflation, and consumers are pressing politicians and regulators to intervene.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Retail power inflation is now a political variable — regulatory intervention risk is rising for anyone earning a margin on US electricity.
insights.quote: US electricity prices are rising at well above the general rate of inflation.

insights.claim: The data centre investment boom adds to electricity demand and points to further upward pressure on US power prices in the future.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The AI capex cycle transmits directly into household utility bills, creating a durable political backlash channel against data centre siting.
insights.quote: The data center investment boom, by adding to electricity demand, points to further upward pressure in the future.

insights.claim: PJM's difficulties have raised concerns among state governors, federal regulators and the White House, elevating a wholesale market design question to the highest level of US politics.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Market-design reform in PJM is now a top-down political process, meaning changes could arrive faster and less predictably than normal RTO stakeholder timelines.
insights.quote: why PJM has raised concerns with among state governors, federal regulators and the White House
insights.locator: PJM offers one of the clearest examples

themes.theme: Competitive market signals no longer working

insights.claim: Competitive power markets such as PJM were designed to lower consumer costs and signal new investment, but in many markets those signals are no longer working as intended.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: If price signals are broken, capacity market outcomes stop being a reliable guide to future supply — model policy intervention instead of clearing prices.
insights.quote: Competitive markets such as PJM were meant to bring down costs for consumers and send the right signals to the industry for new investment. But Carim argues that in many markets, those signals are no longer working as intended.
insights.locator: Competitive markets such as PJM were meant

insights.claim: Reserve margins are tightening and the US industry is struggling to bring new generation online quickly enough, putting system reliability under threat at the same time as bills rise.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Simultaneous reliability and affordability deterioration removes the usual political trade-off and forces structural reform rather than tinkering.
insights.quote: Reserve margins are getting tighter, and the industry is struggling to bring new generation online quickly enough.
insights.locator: Competitive markets such as PJM were meant

insights.claim: US electricity demand is rising at a pace the sector has not seen in decades — driven by data centres, electrification and broader economic growth — and is colliding with a system designed for a very different era.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Treat pre-2020 load-growth assumptions and the market rules built on them as obsolete when underwriting US power assets.
insights.quote: electricity demand is rising at a pace the sector has not seen in decades, driven by data centres, electrification, and broader economic growth
insights.locator: Host Ed Crooks and regular contributor Amy Myers Jaffe

insights.claim: PJM as it has operated until now may not be ready for the demands that AI, electrification and the energy transition are about to place on it.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Expect PJM rule changes to be the template other US markets copy — PJM outcomes are a leading indicator for ERCOT, MISO and beyond.
insights.quote: PJM, as it has operated until now, may not be ready for the demands that AI, electrification and the energy transition are about to place on it.

insights.claim: Exelon's Carim Khouzami argues that regulated utilities, which are often prevented by state rules from owning generation capacity, should be allowed to run their own power plants.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Re-integration would let regulated utilities put generation into rate base — a large potential earnings-growth unlock for wires-only names like Exelon.
insights.quote: Carim makes the case that regulated utilities such as Exelon, which are often prevented by state rules from owning generation capacity, should be allowed to run their own power plants.
insights.locator: The central issue is about the market structures

insights.claim: Khouzami frames the current competitive model as simply not working, making reform the best available option for securing reliability and customer value.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A major utility publicly declaring restructuring a failure signals the industry lobbying position is shifting toward re-regulation, a structural risk to merchant generators.
insights.quote: The current model is not working, he says, and reform is now the best option.

insights.claim: The proposal is made by an executive of Exelon, one of the largest US utility groups and a direct beneficiary of the rule change being advocated.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Discount the advocacy for self-interest, but note that incumbent utilities with the balance sheet to build are the ones lobbying — they usually win these fights.
insights.locator: Host Ed Crooks and regular contributor Amy Myers Jaffe

insights.claim: Amy Myers Jaffe of NYU highlights the risk of overbuilding new power plants and questions whether alternatives such as batteries are being given a fair chance to compete.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Utility-owned generation in rate base has no market discipline against overbuild — stranded-asset and consumer-cost risk is the counterweight to the re-integration case.
insights.quote: Amy highlights the risks of overbuilding new power plants, and asks whether alternative solutions such as batteries are being given a fair chance to compete.
insights.locator: His proposal opens up a wider debate

insights.claim: There is plenty of evidence that competitive power markets have delivered benefits for consumers, leaving open whether they can meet the needs of AI-driven demand growth.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The debate is not restructuring-versus-regulation on merit but whether a model optimised for flat demand can serve rapid growth — a different and narrower test.
insights.quote: There is plenty of evidence that competitive markets have delivered benefits for consumers. But can they meet the needs of the new world of AI-driven demand growth?
insights.locator: His proposal opens up a wider debate

insights.claim: The debate is framed as finding a way to add electricity supply without pushing consumer bills even higher, making cost allocation rather than raw capacity the design problem.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Watch for large-load tariffs and data-centre cost-allocation rules as the practical policy output — that is where the money actually moves.
insights.quote: debates a possible way to add to electricity supplies without pushing bills even higher

insights.claim: Politicians and regulators across the US and around the world will be watching how PJM responds, making it an internationally consequential test of competitive market design.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: PJM's resolution sets precedent for liberalised power markets globally — relevant to European and Australian market-design risk as well.
insights.quote: Politicians and regulators across the US and around the world will be watching to see how it responds.
